ask.text: Suppose you start a new file with Ctrl+N while inside the Shop workspace and never save it, then close and reopen Tinkerdeck. Where should that unsaved file come back?
ask.why: It decides whether Tinkerdeck must remember which workspace a never-saved file belongs to, so it returns to the right strip after a restart; that changes the stored data and what the tests check.

options.label: Back in the Shop workspace's tab strip
options.consequence: Tinkerdeck remembers the workspace of a never-saved file, so it returns where you started it after a restart.

options.label: In the global Editor list with files from no workspace
options.consequence: A never-saved file started inside a workspace leaves that workspace after a restart, and nothing extra is stored.

options.label: Do not reopen never-saved new files at all
options.consequence: A new file you never saved would be gone after a restart, which changes today's promise that typing is never lost.

coverage.note: One local person on their own Windows machine; there are no accounts, roles or sharing.

Being asked: whether a never-saved file's home workspace is stored so the file returns to that workspace after a restart. The workspace config becomes version 2 with a workspaces key and keeps a .bak (decided).
The app has no accounts, roles or sharing; its one user already has full access to the same local files today.

The context menu reuses the explorer's existing name validation and delete warning; reveal and open-terminal validate that the path exists and, for a terminal, stays inside the owning workspace's root.

Existing loading, empty, error and too-large states and wording are kept; the new global list gets an empty message, the menu closes on Escape or outside click, and menu actions are unavailable while an operation is running.
One editor per file in exactly one strip; opening the same path again selects its existing tab instead of making a second copy.

A workspace may hold any number of open editor tabs for the session and the strip scrolls when it overflows; files stay whole-file reads under the existing 5 MB edit cap and only visible lines are drawn.
Closing a tab with unsaved text keeps it in the global Bin for 30 days; deleting a file or folder uses the existing confirm-and-delete action and re-points or closes affected tabs.
No new personal or sensitive data is collected; the same local files are shown that the user can already open.

Exactly one lazily loaded editor surface is reused, terminals stay mounted, and the menu is keyboard-operable (Shift+F10, Menu key, F2, Del) per the request; accessibility, performance and reliability are stated as non-functional requirements.

assumptions: One local person uses Tinkerdeck on their own Windows machine; there are no accounts, roles, sharing or per-file permissions to add.

The explorer and editor keep their existing loading, empty, error and too-large states and wording; the new global file list shows an empty message when no unowned file is open, and the context menu closes on Escape, an outside click or after a choice.

A workspace or the global view keeps every editor tab it has for the session and the tab strip scrolls when it overflows; files remain whole-file reads under the existing 5 MB edit cap, so larger files and logs are not opened here.
